title: Afternoon learning
hook: summer Shabbat afternoons read Pirkei Avot; winter afternoons read psalms

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Shabbat afternoon reading that previews next week. Your line was you start next week before this week ends. Today, what fills the rest of that long afternoon.
screen: `YOU START NEXT WEEK BEFORE THIS WEEK ENDS.`

segments.voice: A summer Saturday, late. The light goes on forever. Lunch was hours ago, and there's still a long stretch before the stars come out and Shabbat ends. No phones, no errands, no work. What do you do with all that time? In some homes and synagogues, the answer is a small book of sayings, read one chapter a week. In winter, when the afternoons are short and dark, the answer changes to psalms. The calendar decides what you study.
screen: `A LONG SUMMER SATURDAY.` → `NO PHONES, NO ERRANDS.` → `THE CALENDAR DECIDES.`

segments.voice: The summer book is Pirkei Avot, the chapters of the fathers, a tractate of the Mishnah made almost entirely of sayings. It opens with a chain: Moses received the Torah at Sinai and handed it on, to Joshua, to the elders, to the prophets, to the great assembly. Then the sages, one by one, each with a line or two. Hillel: if I am not for myself, who will be for me? And if I am only for myself, what am I? And if not now, when? Ben Zoma: who is wise? The one who learns from every person. Who is strong? The one who masters their own impulse. Who is rich? The one who is happy with their portion. The custom is to read one chapter each Shabbat afternoon, starting after Passover. Five chapters come from the Mishnah, and a sixth was added for this reading, so there's about one for each Shabbat between Passover and Shavuot. Some communities keep cycling through the summer until Rosh Hashanah. Then, in winter, Ashkenazi custom often turns to Psalm 104, which praises the whole created world. In the old Jewish translation: "How manifold are Thy works, O LORD!" And to the fifteen Songs of Ascents, Psalms 120 to 134, short songs pilgrims may have sung on the way up to Jerusalem. Why the switch? Customs differ in their reasons, and the sources don't settle it. But the pattern is clear. Long light, practical sayings about how to live. Short light, songs about the world and the climb. Either way, Shabbat afternoon isn't empty time. It's learning time.
screen: `PIRKEI AVOT: A CHAIN FROM SINAI.` · `IF NOT NOW, WHEN?` · `ONE CHAPTER EACH SHABBAT.` · `WINTER: PSALMS OF ASCENTS.` · then, large: `AFTERNOON LEARNING.`

segments.voice: Take one of Ben Zoma's sayings: who is rich? The one who is happy with their portion. Say it slowly, twice, then look around at your portion right now, the room, the people in your life, your body breathing, and let the question sit, without hurrying: is there enough here?
Afternoon learning. Pirkei Avot through the summer Shabbatot, and psalms through the winter ones.
Your line: if not now, when. A week of no requests, V'shamru, Nishmat, seven called, Musaf, Ezra's preview and Avot. Until tomorrow.

howItsDone: Many communities study a chapter of Pirkei Avot each Shabbat afternoon from Passover to Shavuot, and many continue until Rosh Hashanah; in winter, Ashkenazi custom adds Psalm 104 and the Songs of Ascents (Psalms 120–134) after the afternoon service.
